The abstract and introduction are written from the final results; numbers are taken from `results/` as the code produces them, and each description of how a number was computed is confirmed by `experiment-repo` before it goes in.

**Split (`.forgejo/CODEOWNERS` on `dev`)**: `paper/` me; `venue/` (official template, style files, checklist form) `venue-repo`; `figures/`, `tables/` `figtab-repo` (one file per figure/table, named by me in the paper's `\input`/`\includegraphics`, listed in the table below once the outline fixes them); `code/` (incl. `code/README.md` reproduction instructions: environment, data versions, seeds, commands, run time, script per figure/table) and `results/` `experiment-repo`. Build: `cd paper && latexmk -pdf main.tex` -> `paper/main.pdf`.

**Order**: (1) skeleton with venue template and related work from `idea-repo`'s bib; (2) method/protocol/theory text against the experiment code; (3) results sections as numbers arrive; (4) abstract/intro last; (5) offer a candidate to `main` for `internal-review-repo`, answer its review, then `final`.

**Standard**: no number, figure or citation not produced by code or read in the source; failures and unrun experiments stated as such; caveats stated once where they bear on a claim; code/data release stated once.

# Prior work and how the study relates to it

Material for the paper's Related Work and Introduction (delivered by `paper-repo`; `references.bib` holds the entries).
Every item below was looked up (title/abstract/metadata) by this role; the starter-list items were read from `starter_literature.md` descriptions and the abstracts found by search. Items to be cited only after their full text is checked by the writer are marked (verify before citing).

## A. Cheaper evaluation of one benchmark (reduce items, not benchmarks)
- Polo et al. 2024, tinyBenchmarks (arXiv:2402.14992); Vivek et al. 2024, Anchor Points (EACL 2024); Perlitz et al. 2024, Efficient Benchmarking of Language Models (NAACL 2024); Kipnis et al. 2024, metabench (arXiv:2407.12844); Fluid Language Model Benchmarking (arXiv:2509.11106, IRT-based adaptive item selection).
- Relation: they pick *items inside a benchmark* to recover that benchmark's score. We pick *whole benchmarks* to predict *other* benchmarks of a new model. Same spirit (a low-dimensional latent skill explains many scores; IRT and adaptive testing), different unit and target. metabench is the nearest on selection from model-score matrices; its target is the original benchmark's total.

## B. Cross-benchmark predictability and agreement
- Ruan, Maddison, Hashimoto 2024, Observational Scaling Laws (NeurIPS 2024): a few capability principal components from ~100 public models predict downstream scores; Polo et al. 2024, Sloth (arXiv:2412.06540): scaling laws for skills across families; Perlitz et al. 2024, BenchBench (arXiv:2407.13696): benchmark agreement testing and its methodological choices; Hendrycks et al. 2020 (MMLU), Muennighoff et al. 2022 (MTEB), Liang et al. 2022 (HELM), Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench/Arena), Zhuo et al. 2024 (BigCodeBench): the benchmarks and leaderboards that supply data.
- Relation: they show the matrix is low-dimensional and that scores are predictable from compute/family. They take the predictor's input as given (compute, model family or the full set of scores). The open question is the *design*: which k runs, how error falls with k, how it holds up under family or time shift. BenchBench's warning that agreement conclusions depend on protocol choices motivates our family/time-held-out protocol.

## C. Matrix completion and low-rank models with missing entries
- Candès & Recht 2009 (exact matrix completion, uniform random observation); Mazumder, Hastie, Tibshirani 2010 (Soft-Impute); Tipping & Bishop 1999 (probabilistic PCA, EM); Salakhutdinov & Mnih 2007 (PMF); Hernández-Lobato et al. 2014 (PMF with data missing not at random); Udell et al. 2016 (Generalized Low Rank Models).
- Relation: these supply the predictors we compare with and our model (PPCA/EM with missing data). They assume observations are random, while here the new row's observed set is *chosen*, which is our subject. Missingness in leaderboards is not random (MNAR), a limitation we measure.
